title: In re Pharmaceutical Industry Average Wholesale Price Litigation
lead: A drug-pricing settlement promised compensation before directing unclaimed money to cancer-related charities. The First Circuit upheld that negotiated remainder provision after the district court increased members’ recovery.

actors.name: M. Joyce Howe
actors.role: Subclass representative objecting individually and for her husband’s estate

proceedings: Multidistrict litigation produced certification of consumer subclass in January 2006.
District court modified proposed settlement and approved it December 15, 2008.
First Circuit affirmed approval on November 19, 2009.
limits: Estimated $17.2 million claims and $6.8 million charity were projections, not verified final distributions. Decision concerns agreed settlement residue, not court-created charity outside settlement or approval of specific recipients.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Published prices and actual patient losses diverge
paragraphs: Pharmaceutical manufacturers published average wholesale prices used by insurers and Medicare to calculate physician reimbursement and patient co-payments. Plaintiffs alleged manufacturers widened the difference between those figures and physicians’ lower acquisition costs, then marketed that spread to encourage prescriptions. Patients remained charged from the inflated benchmark. This appeal concerned AstraZeneca’s Zoladex, commonly used for prostate cancer, within a much larger pharmaceutical litigation.

A coalition sued in Massachusetts in December 2001, and related cases were consolidated in April 2002. A Medicare Part B co-payment class alleged state consumer-protection violations. Medicare generally paid eighty percent, leaving a twenty-percent co-payment, but most members’ supplemental Medigap policies paid eighty percent of that co-payment. Their actual loss was therefore only the uncovered fraction. Fully covered patients were excluded.

After awaiting suitable representatives, the court certified the class in January 2006, excluding nine states without the relevant statutory action. M. Joyce Howe, individually and for her husband’s estate, and Leroy Townsend represented the AstraZeneca subclass; counsel were appointed.

sections.title: Settlement makes room for a charitable remainder
paragraphs: On the eve of trial in May 2007, the parties settled against estimated losses of $31,128,851. AstraZeneca promised $24 million, including claims for deceased members, and the class expanded to the nine previously excluded states in return for comprehensive peace. Excess claims would be reduced proportionately. Administration and initially negotiated $8.7 million fees and costs were separate obligations, not deductions from that compensation.

With elderly, deceased, and hard-to-locate patients, the agreement used simple claims and minimal proof of Zoladex use. Initial payments doubled estimated actual loss, using average supplemental coverage of eighty percent of co-payments. Unclaimed money would go to mutually acceptable cancer-research or patient-care charities, subject to later judicial recipient approval and an initial $10 million charitable cap.

Howe objected to the expansion, claims process, charity, insurance assumptions, potential subrogation, and fee negotiations. After considering even her tardy reply at the May 2008 fairness hearing, the judge required treble recovery first for the strongest December 1997–2003 claims. In October he extended treble recovery to all members if funds remained after that priority and reduced fees to thirty percent of recovery. The amendment retained a $10 million combined limit for additional treble payments and charity. Final approval followed December 15. A later projection of $17.2 million claims and $6.8 million charity remained an estimate.

sections.title: Compensation precedes charity
paragraphs: Chief Judge Lynch’s unanimous First Circuit panel distinguished charitable substitution when individual distribution is infeasible from disposition of a remainder after compensation. This was the latter. Planning it before claims closed did not change its substance: members could receive treble damages before charity received money, while some patients would never claim.

Howe argued every remaining dollar belonged to claimants and invoked draft aggregate-litigation principles. The court treated those principles as guidance, not binding law. Treble recovery satisfied their compensation concern, and the total also represented losses of nonclaiming patients while preventing AstraZeneca from escaping its agreed payment. Arm’s-length negotiations after adequate discovery supported reasonableness, with judicial examination of benefits, costs, risks, and alternatives still required. Court-created charitable distributions outside settlements remained unresolved, and no particular recipient was approved.

Howe alleged counsel’s prior representation of Prescription Action Litigation diverted loyalty. The court found no evidence that organization promoted charitable funds; it did not fit the agreed cancer-related recipient description. Counsel’s continuing fiduciary duties required scrutiny, but advocating this residue after substantial recovery did not itself establish disloyalty.

sections.title: Alternative payments and preservation
paragraphs: The insurance objection was underdeveloped and waived, and also failed substantively. Insurance-based adjustments matched actual loss. Howe’s policy covered fifty rather than eighty percent of her co-payment, but few members were shown to differ, and enhanced recovery still exceeded loss; plaintiffs estimated she would receive about $200 more. Equal checks using the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services database would misidentify supplemental coverage, pay fully covered nonmembers, and misallocate recovery. Another litigation track’s distribution method did not control these regularly dosed Zoladex claims.

The simultaneous-fee-negotiation objection was not renewed at final approval. A new appellate objection to the amended class definition was also waived, but the panel explained that incorporation of detailed earlier orders could satisfy the rule without repeating everything. Expansion reflected the negotiated demand for total peace. Counsel had in fact been appointed; a further adequacy attack was waived. The panel affirmed the $24 million settlement’s approval, without declaring actual administration complete or validating every possible charitable distribution.
